title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Use the coefficients of Fe and O<sub>2</sub> as the mole ratio, with mol O<sub>2</sub> on top so that mol Fe cancels.
why: The balanced equation says 3 mol O<sub>2</sub> react for every 4 mol Fe, so multiply the moles of Fe by 3/4.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Find the coefficients of propane and water. Set up the mole ratio with mol H<sub>2</sub>O on top and mol C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> on the bottom.
why: One mole of propane makes 4 mol of water (coefficients 1 and 4), so multiply by 4/1; the ratio is exact, so the answer keeps two significant figures like 0.75.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Three substances make three pairs. Each pair's coefficients give one ratio, and each ratio can be written either way up.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Put mol Al on top and mol CuCl<sub>2</sub> on the bottom, using their coefficients from the balanced equation.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: You can go from one product to another: the coefficients of NaCl and CO<sub>2</sub> make the mole ratio. Put mol CO<sub>2</sub> on top.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: Sodium is Na; chlorine is diatomic, Cl<sub>2</sub>; Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> swap-drop to NaCl. Balance first, then use the Cl<sub>2</sub> : NaCl ratio.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Follow the road map: grams CH<sub>4</sub> → mol CH<sub>4</sub> → mol O<sub>2</sub> (mole ratio) → grams O<sub>2</sub>. The goal is the mole.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Grams of CO<sub>2</sub> to moles first. Compare the coefficients of CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O in the glucose equation, then use the molar mass of water.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Road map: grams Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → mol Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → mol Fe (2 Fe per Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) → grams Fe, using the molar mass of Fe from the yellow sheet.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: The desired unit is moles, so stop there: grams KCl → mol KCl → mol AgCl. Count the significant figures in the given mass.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Start on the particle on-ramp: divide molecules by Avogadro's number to get mol NH<sub>3</sub>. Then use the mole ratio and the molar mass of N<sub>2</sub>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Convert mL to L first; then liters × molarity gives moles.
why: Molarity is moles per liter, so 0.0250 L × 0.200 mol/L leaves mol NaOH, with three significant figures.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Use the 1 : 1 ratio between CaCO<sub>3</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>, then 22.4 L/mol, the molar volume of a gas at STP.
why: One mol CaCO<sub>3</sub> gives one mol CO<sub>2</sub>, and at STP each mole of gas fills 22.4 L, so 0.250 mol × 22.4 L/mol gives the volume.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Mol KOH → mol H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> with the 1 : 2 ratio; then liters = moles ÷ molarity. Convert L to mL at the end.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Which substance has the green light (both a volume and a concentration)? Start there: mL → L → mol, then the mole ratio, then ÷ the molarity of AgNO<sub>3</sub>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Find the moles of NH<sub>3</sub> each reactant could make. The reactant that makes less is limiting, and that smaller amount is the product.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Use the limiting reactant's moles to find how much N<sub>2</sub> was used (1 N<sub>2</sub> : 3 H<sub>2</sub>). Excess = initial − used.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Convert each mass to moles, then find the moles of MgO each reactant could make. Do not compare grams; the smaller product amount wins.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Divide each supply by what one sandwich needs. The fewest sandwiches marks the limiting ingredient; leftover = start − used.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Extra step first: mL ethanol × density gives grams. Then find the moles of CO<sub>2</sub> each reactant could make. The two results are close, so carry extra digits.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Percent yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100%. Which number is the actual yield?
why: The actual yield (38.2 g) goes on top and the theoretical yield (45.0 g) on the bottom, so the result is a little below 100%, as expected.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Find the theoretical yield of CaO first (grams CaCO<sub>3</sub> → mol → mol CaO → grams CaO). Then compare grams of CaO with grams of CaO.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: A yield above 100% means the weighed product holds something extra. What could still be in a solid that was dried for only five minutes?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Rearrange: actual yield = (percent yield ÷ 100%) × theoretical yield. Use the unrounded theoretical yield and round once at the end.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Both numbers in a percent yield must be grams of the same product, AlBr<sub>3</sub>. Is 3.00 g of Al a mass of product?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: A positive ΔH means heat is absorbed. For (b) and (c), ask whether the surroundings (your hand, your skin) get warmer or colder.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Grams glucose → mol glucose (molar mass from the yellow sheet), then use 2803 kJ per 1 mol glucose, its coefficient, as the conversion factor.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: ΔH goes with the equation as written, 2 mol H<sub>2</sub>. Use 571.6 kJ / 2 mol H<sub>2</sub> as the conversion factor.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: A negative ΔH means exothermic, so heat is a product: write it on the right side, with no sign. Then pair the heat with the coefficient of H<sub>2</sub>O.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Start with the given, 4.00 g NaOH: grams → mol, then 55.8 kJ released per 1 mol NaOH.

title: Problem 8.1
hint: Put the unit you want (mol O<sub>2</sub>) on top so that mol C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> cancels. Do coefficients count grams or moles?

title: Problem 8.2
hint: One step: multiply by the mole ratio from the coefficients, with mol O<sub>3</sub> on top and mol O<sub>2</sub> on the bottom.

title: Problem 8.3
hint: Glucose has a coefficient of 1. Compare it with the coefficients of CO<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> to build each mole ratio.

title: Problem 8.4
hint: Work backward from the product: how many ethanol molecules does one glucose make? Should you need more or fewer moles of glucose than of ethanol?

title: Problem 8.5
hint: Use two mole ratios, each with 4 mol Al on the bottom: one to O<sub>2</sub> and one to Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.

title: Problem 8.6
hint: Every ratio has 2 mol C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> on the bottom; put 25 mol O<sub>2</sub>, 16 mol CO<sub>2</sub>, or 18 mol H<sub>2</sub>O on top.

title: Problem 8.7
hint: What do the coefficients in a balanced equation count? In a reaction, which quantities are always conserved: atoms, mass, or moles?

title: Problem 8.8
hint: Balance first: FeCl<sub>3</sub> has 3 Cl and Cl<sub>2</sub> has 2, so even the odds on Cl (6). Then use the balanced Fe : Cl<sub>2</sub> and Fe : FeCl<sub>3</sub> ratios.

title: Problem 8.9
hint: Road map: grams H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → mol H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → mol O<sub>2</sub> (2 : 1) → grams O<sub>2</sub>. The goal is the mole.

title: Problem 8.10
hint: Set up grams → mol → mol → grams with the 3 : 1 mole ratio. Watch for choices that skip the ratio, flip it, or put a coefficient into a molar mass.

title: Problem 8.11
hint: Grams NH<sub>3</sub> → mol NH<sub>3</sub> → mol urea (2 NH<sub>3</sub> per urea) → grams urea. Watch how you show three significant figures for a number that ends in zero.

title: Problem 8.12
hint: Grams Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> → mol → mol CO<sub>2</sub> (1 : 1) → grams CO<sub>2</sub>. Keep three significant figures, like 1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> g.

title: Problem 8.13
hint: Grams glucose → mol → mol O<sub>2</sub> (6 : 1) → grams O<sub>2</sub>. To check, find the masses of CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O too: reactant mass should equal product mass.

title: Problem 8.14
hint: Grams Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → mol, then 2 mol Al per 1 mol Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, then the molar mass of Al. Grams of A never go straight to grams of B.

title: Problem 8.15
hint: (a) Look at the last factor: does a molar mass change with the coefficient? (c) The MgO mass must equal the Mg mass plus the O<sub>2</sub> used.

title: Problem 8.16
hint: Find mol KClO<sub>3</sub> once, then use two mole ratios: 3 O<sub>2</sub> : 2 KClO<sub>3</sub> and 2 KCl : 2 KClO<sub>3</sub>. Check that the two masses add up to the starting mass.

title: Problem 8.17
hint: Grams Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> → mol → mol HCl (3 : 1); then liters = moles ÷ molarity. Convert to mL at the end.

title: Problem 8.18
hint: Grams Mg → mol Mg → mol H<sub>2</sub> (compare those two coefficients) → liters with 22.4 L/mol. Would a small strip of ribbon make liters or milliliters of gas?

title: Problem 8.19
hint: HCl has the green light (a volume and a concentration): mL → L → mol HCl, then 1 : 1 to NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, then its molar mass.

title: Problem 8.20
hint: 22.4 L/mol applies only to a gas at STP (0 °C and 1 atm). Check each choice for both: is it a gas, and is it at STP?

title: Problem 8.21
hint: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> has the green light: mL → L → mol, then 2 HCl per Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>, then ÷ the molarity of HCl.

title: Problem 8.22
hint: (a) Grams glucose → mol → mol O<sub>2</sub> (6 : 1) → liters with 22.4 L/mol. (b) Compare the coefficients of O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>.

title: Problem 8.23
hint: CaCl<sub>2</sub> has the green light: convert 20.0 mL to liters first, find mol CaCl<sub>2</sub>, then use 2 AgCl per CaCl<sub>2</sub> and the molar mass of AgCl.

title: Problem 8.24
hint: At the same temperature and pressure, the mole ratio is also a volume ratio, so (a) and (b) need no 22.4. For (c): liters → mol with 22.4 L/mol → grams.

title: Problem 8.25
hint: Run each reactant to the same product: the moles of H<sub>2</sub>O each could make. The smaller amount marks the limiting reactant; mass alone does not decide.

title: Problem 8.26
hint: Find the moles of NO each reactant could make. Equal moles of reactants do not mean neither limits; the coefficients 4 and 5 differ.

title: Problem 8.27
hint: Count recipes: each O<sub>2</sub> uses 2 CO and makes 2 CO<sub>2</sub>. How many O<sub>2</sub> would 8 CO need? Remember to show any leftover molecules.

title: Problem 8.28
hint: Find the moles of H<sub>2</sub> each could make: Mg by its molar mass, HCl by liters × molarity. The smaller wins; excess = initial − used.

title: Problem 8.29
hint: For each row, NH<sub>3</sub> from N<sub>2</sub> = mol N<sub>2</sub> × 2/1 and from H<sub>2</sub> = mol H<sub>2</sub> × 2/3. The smaller wins; then find how much of the other reactant it used.

title: Problem 8.30
hint: Convert both masses to moles (1 : 1 ratios), then to grams of FeS. The reactant that makes less FeS limits; a smaller mass does not mean fewer moles.

title: Problem 8.31
hint: Find the moles of Cu each reactant could make (3 Cu : 2 Al; 3 Cu : 3 CuCl<sub>2</sub>). Then use the limiting reactant to find the Al used; excess = initial − used.

title: Problem 8.32
hint: Grams to moles for each, then the moles of NH<sub>3</sub> each could make. The smaller wins, even if it is the bigger mass. Excess H<sub>2</sub> = initial − used, in grams.

title: Problem 8.33
hint: Find the moles of SO<sub>2</sub> each reactant could make, using the 2 : 2 and 2 : 3 ratios. Comparing 2.0 with 2.4 directly ignores the recipe.

title: Problem 8.34
hint: Percent yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100%. Which number did the student collect?

title: Problem 8.35
hint: Find the theoretical yield of acetaminophen from 4-aminophenol first (grams → mol → mol → grams). Then actual on top, theoretical on the bottom.

title: Problem 8.36
hint: (a) Theoretical yield = g Al ÷ 26.98 g/mol × 474.37 g/mol (1 mol Al gives 1 mol alum); then actual ÷ theoretical × 100%. (b) Look for a yield that cannot happen.

title: Problem 8.37
hint: Find the theoretical yield of MgO from the Mg first (grams → mol → mol → grams). The mass weighed afterward is the actual yield; it goes on top.

title: Problem 8.38
hint: A yield above 100% needs extra mass in the weighed product. Which choice adds mass instead of losing product?

title: Problem 8.39
hint: Work backward: theoretical yield = actual ÷ percent × 100%. Then go from grams of aspirin back to grams of salicylic acid (1 : 1).

title: Problem 8.40
hint: All the ratios are 1 : 1, so compare the moles of the two reactants; the smaller limits and sets the theoretical yield. Then actual ÷ theoretical × 100%.

title: Problem 8.41
hint: Step 2 can only work on the product step 1 made. Try it with 100 g: how much is left after step 1, and then after step 2?

title: Problem 8.42
hint: The pack warms your skin, so which way does heat flow? Heat leaving the system goes with which sign of ΔH?

title: Problem 8.43
hint: Grams propane → mol propane, then 2.220 × 10<sup>3</sup> kJ per 1 mol C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>. Use scientific notation to show three significant figures.

title: Problem 8.44
hint: ΔH goes with the equation as written: 571.6 kJ per 2 mol H<sub>2</sub>. Convert grams to moles first, and check the sign: released or absorbed?

title: Problem 8.45
hint: Grams CaCO<sub>3</sub> → mol, then 178 kJ per 1 mol CaCO<sub>3</sub>. A positive ΔH tells you which way the heat flows.

title: Problem 8.46
hint: (a) Grams glucose → mol, then 2803 kJ per 1 mol glucose. (b) Divide kilojoules by 4.184 kJ per Cal.

title: Problem 8.47
hint: Two changes: reversing an equation changes the sign of ΔH, and doubling it doubles ΔH. Apply both.

title: Problem 8.48
hint: Grams NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> → mol, then 25.7 kJ per 1 mol. A positive ΔH means heat is absorbed.

title: Problem 8.49
hint: Gas volume at STP → mol with 22.4 L/mol, then 890.3 kJ per 1 mol CH<sub>4</sub>. Count the significant figures in 250. L.

title: Problem 8.50
hint: (a) Swap-drop Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Cl<sup>−</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup>, PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>. (b) Balance Ca and PO<sub>4</sub> first. (c) Find the moles of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> each reactant could make; the smaller sets the theoretical yield.

title: Problem 8.51
hint: (a) Complete combustion makes CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O; balance C, then H, then O. (b) Find the moles of CO<sub>2</sub> each reactant could make. (d) Pair ΔH with the limiting reactant.

title: Problem 8.52
hint: (a) Two NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> balance one SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>. (b) Find the moles of product each reactant could make; the bigger mass does not decide. (e) Excess = initial − used.

title: Problem 8.53
hint: (a) Fe<sup>3+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> swap-drop; balance O first. (b) Grams Fe → mol, then 1648 kJ per 4 mol Fe. (c) Mol Fe → mol O<sub>2</sub> → liters at STP.

title: Problem 8.54
hint: Find mol glucose once. (a) 2 ethanol per glucose, then grams. (b) 2 CO<sub>2</sub> per glucose, then 22.4 L/mol. (c) Actual ÷ theoretical × 100%. (d) Yeast are alive.

title: Problem 8.55
hint: (a) Carbonates give a salt, H<sub>2</sub>O, and CO<sub>2</sub>. (b) mg ÷ g/mol gives mmol; then use the HCl mole ratio. (c) For per gram, divide mmol HCl by grams of ingredient.

title: Problem 8.56
hint: Use only the ratio that links H<sub>2</sub>O and O<sub>2</sub>, with the unit you want, mol O<sub>2</sub>, on top.

title: Problem 8.57
hint: Map: grams ethanol → mol ethanol → mol O<sub>2</sub> → molecules O<sub>2</sub>. Avogadro's number is the off-ramp after the mole ratio.

title: Problem 8.58
hint: CaCl<sub>2</sub> has the green light: find its moles first. (a) Use 2 Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> : 3 CaCl<sub>2</sub>, then ÷ molarity. (b) Use 1 Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> : 3 CaCl<sub>2</sub>.

title: Problem 8.59
hint: Amounts of both reactants are given, so it is a limiting-reactant problem. Extra step first: mL acetic acid × density = grams. Then compare the moles of CO<sub>2</sub> each could make.

title: Problem 8.60
hint: Find the theoretical yield of ZnCl<sub>2</sub> from the zinc first. Then actual ÷ theoretical × 100%; never divide grams of a reactant by grams of product.

title: Problem 8.61
hint: Find the theoretical yield of NH<sub>3</sub> from 50.0 g N<sub>2</sub> first; then actual = (percent ÷ 100%) × theoretical.

title: Problem 8.62
hint: (a) Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> give MgO; oxygen is O<sub>2</sub>. Exothermic, so heat is a product. (b) Pair 1203 kJ with 2 mol Mg. (c) Start with 300. kJ; pair it with 2 mol MgO.

title: Problem 8.63
hint: Heat written on the reactant side is absorbed. Which sign goes with absorbed heat? Does ΔH belong to the equation as written or to one mole of NO?
